I’ll read the handoff, manuscripts, and three registers, then trace each proposed witness back to the cut or disk its source actually supplies. I’ll send bounded derivations for independent review before integrating any result.

The three-handle calculation gives a new reduction from the upper end. A certificate on the level after two attachments can lower the middle count from three to two even when the first cut is unresolved. On the analytic side, I’m checking whether a curved Euclidean ball can replace the charged disk using data measured on its boundary.

The upper cancellation now extends to any upper handlebody rank when the penultimate lower sublevel is simply connected and its boundary is PSC-dominated. The disk calculation also exposed a limitation of the immersion route: on a transverse nonround convex height slice, the natural Euclidean filling has the wrong trace-free second fundamental form. I’ll include both results and their hypotheses in the manuscripts.

**A positive-scalar-curvature witness on the penultimate cut can force a net handle cancellation.** Suppose the sublevel through all but the last middle handle is simply connected, the upper handlebody has positive rank, and its boundary cut receives a nonzero-degree map from a closed oriented PSC three-manifold. Then the last 2-handle cancels an upper 3-handle on the original smooth four-manifold. The proof tracks the inverse gluing and works at every upper rank. [Surgery manuscript](sandbox:/Users/ebbaker/Documents/smooth-poincare-4d/output/pdf/05_collar_deformation_and_surgery/02_handle_isolation_and_marked_surgery/recognition_from_marked_handle_cuts.pdf)

For one lower and three middle handles, the two tests give different successors. A witness after the first winding-one attachment returns a one-sided two-component link, with both framed tubes transported. A witness after the second attachment returns a mixed two-middle presentation, even when the first cut fails. The stabilized Mazur double realizes this distinction. On the original double, the **meridian-first** cut carries the constructed global PSC metric’s degree-one stable separator and measured product band. The long-handle-first cut fails PSC domination.

**On the charged disk**, a curved Euclidean filling extends the fixed-index obstruction to certain nonumbilic boundaries. Matching the trace-free second fundamental forms and satisfying the boundary mean-curvature inequality forces both disk masses to be at most the minimizing excess \(e_i-I^+(M)\). A transverse nonround convex immersion level fails that matching test for its own Euclidean filling. No qualifying fill or coupled saving was found on the original minimizing sequence. I’ll replay the previous milestone against the current files, then pursue a two-attachment move and a finite-width disk comparison in parallel. For each, I’ll track which presentation or physical metric supplies the evidence.

The surgery sources give a way to test two attachments together even when the first cut fails the PSC test. On the disk side, the first calculation gives a separate price for each chirality: a fixed trace-free mismatch contributes energy of order \(1/w\) on a collar of width \(w\). I’m checking both results against the actual markings and the complete exterior.

The marked example now has a measured witness. Both original first cuts fail PSC domination for the selected band. Undoing the slide exposes the unknot-first cut, where a round band of total width \(\pi/12\) passes the two-end mean-curvature test. Separately, a hyperbolic cap fits a nonround ellipsoid height; I’m checking exactly which boundary data that construction would require on the minimizing disk.

The independent readers confirmed the band calculation, both cancellations, and the finite-width cap estimate. The ellipsoid comparison also passes with both chiralities charged on both sides. For the selected minimizing disk, the available data still leave the boundary shape and affordable width undetermined. I’ve incorporated those distinctions into the manuscripts, including the inverse map after the three-to-two reduction.

**A marked two-attachment move crosses a level where both individual PSC tests fail.** For a selected band in the Gompf–Scharlemann–Thompson square-knot diagram, both possible first attachments have boundaries that admit no PSC-dominating map. Undoing the slide exposes the unknot-first cut. On that returned cut, a round band of total width \(\pi/12\) passes the two-end mean-curvature test, even though its width alone is insufficient. The closed one-lower, three-middle example carries both residual framed tubes through the first cancellation and reduces \(3\to2\to0\), with the inverse gluing tracked throughout. genui{"citation":{"refs":["turn668032973view2","turn668032973view3","turn263588538view1"]}}

**A curved reference succeeds on a nonround immersed height.** A near-round ellipsoid admits an exact hyperbolic cap after conformal normalization. Both complete sides carry positive Weyl energy in both chiralities. At a positive physical width, the replacement saves energy in both signs, retains the entire exterior, and keeps the whole joined path below \(8\pi^2\).

**The selected Yamabe minimizing disk remains open.** For a convex reference inducing its actual face metric, the leading connector cost in *each* chirality is
\[
\frac{\|(x\chi)''\|_2^2}{4w}\,\|K^\circ-S^\circ\|_{L^2}^2.
\]
The available disk data do not bound this mismatch at a width where the capped exterior is positive and the saving is strict. For an overlapping deformation, the new estimate identifies a cost that must appear either in the isolated disk-side connector at the endpoint or in the two connectors at an earlier energy crossing. It retains the protected-core mass. Handle selection, positive subcritical entry, and smooth compactness of the physical marking remain separate open steps toward SPC4.
